source.title: NonTextual Target Attack
source.authors: Xinzhe Huang; Wenjing Hu; Ke-Dong Xiu; Hong-Sheng Hu; Xiaojun Jia; Zhan Qin; Tian-Hang Zheng

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffix jailbreaks elicit harmful responses, using a new suffix-optimization method and attack-success measures rather than fine-tuning or measuring per-token KL.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates jailbreak success from adversarial prompts, including suffix attacks, but does not test fine-tuning, compliant prefilling, decoding changes, response-position KL, safety-related parameter localization, or training to deepen safety. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. Response-diversity results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Reports how often adversarial-suffix prompts make safety-aligned open models (Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Vicuna-7B) give harmful responses, plus transfer to larger models. That is a rate of the V4 behaviour (suffixes defeat refusal). It is a new attack method rather than the originals' prefill or KL method. The evidence is weak: there is no no-attack baseline, success is cumulative over up to 100 optimisation attempts per prompt, and it comes from sampled decoding (temperature 0.7, top-k 10).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that NTA, a gradient suffix attack maximising a classifier's unsafe score instead of forcing a fixed affirmative prefix, reaches higher ASR in only 100 iterations than state-of-the-art attacks. They also argue that fixed-target (prefix) objectives over-constrain the search and can collapse, and they report robustness across judges, defenses and scoring models, plus some transfer.
record.recipe_differences: Uses gradient-based optimization of adversarial suffixes to maximize unsafe-response scoring; it does not fine-tune the safety-trained model or measure token-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with dataset, defense, external judge, and transfer target. In the reported Llama3 scoring-model ablation, success remains high across the four scoring models.

fits_no_version.finding: Suffix optimisation that targets an unsafe-classifier score, with no compliant-prefix target, beats prefix-targeted GCG and AdvPrefix at 100 iterations; GCG reaches only 39% ASR-G on Llama3. The paper also illustrates prefix-forced responses reverting to refusal ('Sure... but I can't help').
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Defeating refusal does not require forcing a compliant opening; objectives that force an affirmative prefix can fail because models recover after it.

fits_no_version.finding: NTA responses are more semantically diverse than baseline attacks' responses (Qwen: DNS 0.80, ADN 0.91, Self-BLEU 0.44; Table 10, Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diversity of jailbroken outputs; not a claim version.

record.problems: The principal benchmark results use randomly sampled subsets of 100 prompts per dataset. Attack success is judged by classifiers; no uncertainty estimates are reported. Transfer success is much lower than the white-box results, and defense and independent-judge evaluations show lower success in some conditions.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted the baseline attack rows from Tables 1-5 and scoring-model sensitivity rows for target models other than Llama3 in Table 7. Also omitted the cumulative iteration curve in Figure 4 and the average reported in the text because these are aggregate or figure-based results and the tables provide more condition-specific outcomes.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or any position-wise analysis of aligned vs base models.

Prefilling a compliant start and decoding-change attacks are not tested. The paper also does not test whether the suffix works by changing the opening tokens; NTA deliberately places no constraint on response prefixes.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
No deepening defences. The defenses tested (perplexity filter, SmoothLLM, paraphrase) are input-side, not alignment training.

missing.what: No no-attack (plain harmful prompt) ASR is reported for any target model, so the gain attributable to the suffix cannot be computed. This is a gap in the paper, not an extraction omission.

record.verdict_notes: This is an attack-method paper; its V4 relevance is only that optimised suffixes defeat refusal on aligned models. Rows r21-r31 and r44-r45 duplicate the Table 1 values and should not be counted as independent evidence. Neither original source is this paper. The text cites Qi et al. 2023 only for the judge prompt. Possible table-label inconsistency: the Table 1 header groups DRL/ECLIPSE/PAIR under unlimited tokens, but column alignment in the extracted text is garbled; the NTA values were verified against the prose (95/97 on Llama3 AdvBench).

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and refusal after fine-tuning.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Tests adversarial suffix attacks; does not test compliant prefilling or decoding changes.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or the training objective produces shallow safety.
Training to spread safety beyond the first tokens and whether that holds up.

relationships.condition: White-box NTA suffix attacks on Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, Mistral-7B-Instruct and Vicuna-7B; AdvBench and HarmBench 100-prompt subsets; GPTFuzzer and HarmBench-classifier judges; up to 100 iterations
relationships.reason: ASR is 86-99% across models, datasets and scoring models (r01-r20, r46-r51). There is no no-attack baseline, and Mistral/Vicuna are weakly aligned.
relationships.display_finding: ASR was 86–99% across models, datasets and judges, with no no-attack baseline, and Mistral and Vicuna are weakly aligned.

relationships.condition: Llama3-8B with SmoothLLM or paraphrase input defenses
relationships.reason: ASR-H falls from 97% to 79% (SmoothLLM) and 61% (paraphrase); the perplexity filter has no effect (r32-r34).
relationships.display_finding: Attack success fell from 97% to 79% under SmoothLLM and to 61% under paraphrasing, while the perplexity filter had no effect.

relationships.condition: Llama3-8B AdvBench responses rescored by external LLM judges
relationships.reason: Success depends on the judge: 82% (GPT-4o), 56% (Gemini-2.5-pro), 64% (Claude-Sonnet-4.5) vs 95-97% with the primary classifiers (r35-r37).
relationships.display_finding: Success was 82% with GPT-4o, 56% with Gemini-2.5-pro and 64% with Claude-Sonnet-4.5 as judge, versus 95–97% with the primary classifiers.

relationships.condition: Suffixes optimised on white-box models and transferred one-query to Llama3-70B-it, DeepSeek-R1-671B and Grok-3
relationships.reason: Transferred suffixes succeed only 20-35% of the time on these larger or closed models (r38-r43).
relationships.display_finding: Transferred one-query suffixes succeeded only 20–35% of the time on these larger or closed models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: NTA suffix attacks on the five open-source target models, AdvBench and HarmBench, 100 optimization iterations; also default-configuration AdvBench results and Llama3 scoring-model ablations
reader_labels.reason: High attack success rates are reported across the main benchmark conditions and scoring models (r01-r30, r44-r51).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama3 after SmoothLLM or paraphrase defenses; external judges; transfer to advanced target models
reader_labels.reason: Attack success is lower under some defenses and judges, and transfer results are substantially below the main white-box results (r33-r37, r38-r43).
